title: Can a platform worker deactivated by an algorithm obtain genuine human review before losing their livelihood?
description: A board-level oversight question testing whether a platform's worker-facing algorithmic decisions come with real disclosure and human review, not a process courts might find symbolic.
question_text: If our platform's algorithm restricts, penalises, or deactivates a worker's account, is the worker told the specific basis and given a human review with real authority to reverse the decision — or would a court, as happened to Uber in Amsterdam, find our review 'not much more than a purely symbolic act'?
rationale: Two independent EU court rulings — against Uber in Amsterdam and Deliveroo in Bologna — found that algorithmic management systems penalising or deactivating workers without genuine disclosure and human review violated worker protections.
follow_up_actions: Request the current worker algorithmic decision appeal log and confirm reversal rates are non-trivial.
Confirm workers are told the specific automated basis for a decision, not a generic explanation.
Ask whether scoring logic distinguishes legally protected non-performance (illness, protected activity) from unjustified non-performance.

citations.title: Rb. Amsterdam, 14 April 2021 — C/13/696010 / HA ZA 21-81
